Our goal with [UI3, our latest interface for Figma](https://www.figma.com/blog/behind-our-redesign-ui3/)

, is to keep designers in the flow by minimizing distractions and placing their work center stage. With that north star in mind, our team worked for over two years, iterating on myriad approaches—even reversing some core design decisions, like the floating navigation and properties panels, after launch. It’s all been in service of delivering the next generation of Figma UI to the millions of people who use it everyday. “Craft and flow don’t have easy metrics, so you have to listen to users a lot, and then process feedback carefully,” says Marcin Wichary, Design Director at Figma.

We’ve learned that redesigning for designers means setting a destination, but making sure everyone is along for the journey. **As we make UI3 available for all users on October 10**, we’re sharing how craft, metrics, intuition, and feedback serve as crucial guideposts along the way.

## [Docked panels: Embracing the opportunity to explore](#docked-panels-embracing-the-opportunity-to-explore)

Intimidating as it may be to redesign a product for designers, it’s also a rare opportunity to “revisit things that feel un-revisitable,” says Marcin. “You get to ponder whether something actually works, or if it wasn’t that great to begin with, or if we’ve just gotten weirdly used to it. There are never easy answers, but the questions are fascinating.”

Joel Miller, Product Designer at Figma, adds, “This was a rare opportunity to challenge the status quo, experiment with bolder ideas, and potentially reshape the way people interact with Figma.” The team debated some “wild concepts,” especially around the navigation and properties panels, which are a foundational part of the interface. In some explorations, the panels only appeared on hover; in others, they hung above the canvas. “When you play it safe, you may not know where the ceiling is,” says KC Oh, Product Manager at Figma. We landed on the idea of floating panels, creating a simplified, friendly interface that persists across our product ecosystem—but knew that feedback would tell us if this was too far a departure.

Figma’s floating UI isn’t going away entirely. Panels will float in Figma Design with Minimize UI, in Figma Slides in grid view, and in FigJam as a default. Toolbars will float at the bottom of all Figma products.

It wasn’t until we released UI3 in open beta that we could fully measure the impact through feature adoption, performance metrics, and user feedback. It became clear that though the floating panels were exciting for some, they hindered people who spend many hours a day in Figma. We heard that they cramped the canvas, especially on smaller screens, and that designs seemed to peek out from behind them in a way that was distracting. They also made rulers less effective by moving them further away from designs. “We want Figma to be fast. Speed is a feature,” says KC. “The nail in the coffin was learning that they slowed people down.” For the full rollout of UI3, we’re reversing the change so that panels are fixed, but still resizable to allow for greater flexibility.

## [Minimize UI: Steering toward a singular vision](#minimize-ui-steering-toward-a-singular-vision)

“With every creative project, you have to have a belief about the world and how it’s changing, which guides your approach,” says Ryhan Hassan, Product Designer at Figma. Though we had carte blanche with the new interface, we had several years’ worth of user feedback to parse. In riffing on solutions to these problems, a core insight emerged: Though UI patterns and interactions may evolve in years to come, the idea that work should be the center of the canvas will remain true.

> With every creative project, you have to have a belief about the world and how it’s changing.

Ryhan Hassan, Product Designer, Figma

This led us to question where the UI was necessary at all. Though the existing Hide UI feature put work front and center, some users found it to be blunt and limiting. The new Minimize UI feature adds flexibility by collapsing the side panels for distraction-free work, but allowing users to easily access tools when needed. It’s also smoother to navigate on small and split-screen scenarios, which is more common with remote and hybrid work.

For when UI does come into play, we rearranged some features for a cleaner hierarchy that also leaves logical places for future capabilities to slot in. “Before the redesign, we found ourselves playing Tetris while fitting in new features,” says Ryhan. Now, for instance, the navigation panel linearly lists the file name, branch name, and project name, followed by pages and layers. “As we introduce more ways to move around the file, we have a logical place for those to extend without hard tradeoffs,” says Ryhan. “Overall, there’s a progression toward what we can’t achieve yet.”

## [Blend modes: Bridging past and present](#blend-modes-bridging-past-and-present)

“Broadly speaking, we’ve filed away some of the training wheels of interfaces,” says Marcin. “For example, Shift-based command shortcuts are now commonplace even though they are ostensibly _wrong_ if you think about how keyboards work. Semi-invisible scrollbars are all around us.” It was a fun challenge to negotiate these evolving trends for UI3, and how they impact blend modes in particular, he says. “Some of the conventions around blend modes go back to the ’90s, long before Figma could’ve even been imagined.”

![One iteration of the blend modes UI placed it behind a droplet icon.](data:image/png;base64,)![One iteration of the blend modes UI placed it behind a droplet icon.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/0c39feeb3433c21a816998b3083202b16093e2cc-1080x864.png?w=804&h=643&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

An early iteration had blend modes behind an icon button.

In an early pass, the team placed this control behind an icon button, which would reveal a menu. Changing the blend mode from the default would also change the icon. While this approach simplified the appearance panel—one of the goals of the redesign—it slowed down workflows because it forced users to wait for a tooltip above the icon to know what blend mode was set. Now when users choose any nonstandard blend mode, an inline dropdown makes it easy to change or remove the setting. It’s a solution that keeps the UI minimal while harkening back to the early days of blend mode.

## [Properties panel: Building with your users](#properties-panel-building-with-your-users)

“We’re constantly in a balancing act, trying to push as far as we can while making sure that UI3 logically progresses for people coming from the old interface,” says Ryhan. But after years of working on something, it’s easy to get caught up in your own perspective. “That’s why it’s crucial to regularly gather feedback from the community and, just as importantly, show them that you’re acting on it,” says Joel. “The best products are built not just by the team behind them, but in close collaboration with the people who use them.”

Evolving the properties panel at large, we focused on prioritizing component controls, unifying all the new layout-related options, and revisiting the header. Incorporating feedback since launch, we’ve also changed constraints to be expanded by default, added library information for components, and updated Auto Layout controls to always show pixel values and resize mode. “We make sure we’re trying things, showing how we’re iterating, and listening to a broad range of people,” says Ryhan.

![Four explorations of clip content float over an orange background.](data:image/png;base64,)![Four explorations of clip content float over an orange background.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/1ad0f04af769e7ed1b4aea813f1b4bc09e5d713c-1056x704.png?w=804&h=536&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

Explorations of clip content that didn’t make the cut

**Clip content** allows you to hide parts of a layer that extend beyond the bounds of the parent frame.

For clip content, the team investigated a slew of ways to better fit it into the updated properties panel and solve some long-standing problems. In one iteration, clip content became a toggle with an icon; in others, an icon button or a menu. For the public beta, clip content was a dropdown option, but it caused an extra click that slowed down workflows. We’ve gone back to the checkbox as the most clear, efficient control—and updated it visually to rebalance with the rest of the interface. “It might have felt like a defeat, arriving in almost the same place where we started,” says Marcin. “But better to have riffed and lost, than to never have riffed at all, right?”

Balancing user feedback with design intuition raises essential questions. “Let’s say we get some critical feedback,” Marcin continues. “Is that just a natural reaction to change, or is there something long-lasting here? Does this feed into some of the self-critique we’ve already built up on this idea? Is the negative feedback matched by positive feedback in the right ratio? It feels somewhat familiar, because that’s the job of each designer leaving a [design crit](https://www.figma.com/blog/design-critiques-at-figma/)

—but now times a thousand.”

## [Sliders: Mobilizing the whole team](#sliders-mobilizing-the-whole-team)

Speaking of design crits, even those had to evolve to accommodate UI3’s pressing needs. Instead of the usual 30-minute, individualized design crits, the team developed 60-minute “speed rounds” to address the sheer amount of surfaces being reimagined for UI3, with everyone commenting on each other’s work at once. “This was two months of intense exploration,” says KC. “The entire team mobilized.”

Zooming in on one of many comment threads

Speed rounds allowed designers to load-balance and self-select: Some focused on visual details, and others on flows and the bigger picture. For Wayne Sun, Product Designer at Figma, these crits helped revisit core building blocks like the slider component. The process revealed all the contexts it needed to adapt to: showing numeric values in video scrubbing, notches when adjusting variable fonts, and hue and opacity previews in manipulating color. For good measure, it also needed to fit within a whole new product, [Figma Slides](https://www.figma.com/blog/figma-slides/)

.

![Three slider variants show a slider with a blue fill, a slider with dot steppers, and a slider with a gradient color fill.](data:image/png;base64,)![Three slider variants show a slider with a blue fill, a slider with dot steppers, and a slider with a gradient color fill.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/f934471f72340d103689ca703bb9cc50593ba1f0-1080x864.png?w=804&h=643&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

The team riffed on variants like slider range (A), slider stepper (B), and slider color (C).

## [Labels: Grounding decisions in solid reasoning](#labels-grounding-decisions-in-solid-reasoning)

“For designers living in these tools day in and day out, even a tiny change can feel like a major upheaval,” says Joel. “It’s intimidating—you start wondering, what if this goes horribly wrong? What if I’ve completely missed the mark? That’s why every change needs to be grounded in a solid, sensible motivation that genuinely improves efficiency or coherence.”

Hoi Fung Ho, UX Writer at Figma, experienced this when proposing a new labeling system to help people wayfind, aimed at simplicity without sacrificing clarity. “I’ve never seen a system with optional labels, so this proposal made me spin with self doubt,” she says.

![Screenshots of the proposed UI show the Auto Layout panel with tooltips that read “vertical.”](data:image/png;base64,)![Screenshots of the proposed UI show the Auto Layout panel with tooltips that read “vertical.”](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/2ebec7a2632c02dfc0fb6a726610ca93b2c71fe8-1080x864.png?w=804&h=643&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

In the proposal, the label uses a noun (“padding”), and the tooltip describes a direction (“vertical”).

![The new UI uses tooltips that say “vertical padding” and “vertical layout.”](data:image/png;base64,)![The new UI uses tooltips that say “vertical padding” and “vertical layout.”](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/ec5404ff50a4ecbb87ad0b2ed12f12118ca091a8-1080x864.png?w=804&h=643&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

In the new UI, visible labels match aria-labels used for screen readers.

![Several icons, like a sun, crescent moon, light bulb, and globe are placed on white and black backgrounds.](data:image/png;base64,)![Several icons, like a sun, crescent moon, light bulb, and globe are placed on white and black backgrounds.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/0b52fcc53bfba98244fe2c25b3313ecfcc327f8a-1840x1845.png?w=1840&h=1845&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

Product Designer Tim Van Damme hand-drew 200 icons to convey different controls, including these directions for dark and light mode.

Particularly hard to untangle was the intersection of new labels and existing tooltips. An early minimalistic approach showed promise, but the team later learned that it would hurt accessibility. “This was a deal breaker,” says Hoi. “I quickly revised the approach, which I was glad to do because being able to definitively say ‘This is what we’re doing, and here’s why’ melted the doubts away.” Now, all labels provide the full context, which has a benefit of also making them easier to implement.

The labels were crucial for going from cruft to craft, and the overall quality of the new interface. They compounded Wayne’s work on UI controls, Tim’s overhaul of iconography, Joel’s push for a better properties panel, Ryhan’s focus on overall vision, and many other Figma designers’ contributions.

## [Change management: Giving users time to adapt](#change-management-giving-users-time-to-adapt)

But, ultimately, any new interface is never about us. “Redesigns are fun for designers, but can be genuinely scary for users,” says Marcin. “It _never_ feels like the right time.”

That’s why we gave users a way to opt out of UI3 while it’s in beta: so they could familiarize themselves with the new interface at their own pace. “If you get UI3 on a Wednesday, but have a work deadline for Friday, you can still go back to the old version and get things done,” says Ryhan. The gradual rollout also lets us learn from user experiences, have time to process feedback, and build a body of tutorials, ensuring that answers are readily available when UI3 becomes the default and the old interface is eventually deprecated.

“But we hope,” says Marcin, “that you’ll come back. We think there’s a lot to love about UI3, and we’re not even finished.”

“Except for clip content,” adds Joel. “We’re definitely done with that.”

[As you explore UI3](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/23954856027159-Navigating-UI3-Figma-s-new-UI), available for all users on October 10, keep the feedback coming. Your insights are shaping the future of our design tools, one pixel at a time.
